lead: A radar is not only a block diagram. The antenna must form a narrow beam and scan it, the transmitter must deliver a short high-power pulse, and the receiver must hear a very weak echo. A duplexer lets both share one antenna without burning the receiver. Modulators shape the pulse, displays turn echoes into a map, and the atmosphere bends and attenuates the wave. This chapter connects the blocks to real hardware: dish and array antennas, tubes and solid-state transmitters, superheterodyne receivers, TR tubes, PPI displays, and the propagation effects an operator sees.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the block diagram, Unit 3 for reflectors and arrays, Unit 4 for tubes and circulators, and Unit 5 for receivers and noise.

sections.h3: Antennas: dish, shaped beam and array

blocks.text: A radar needs a high-gain antenna with low sidelobes. A parabolic reflector puts a small feed at the focus. The feed illuminates the dish, and the dish forms a narrow pencil beam. Some radars scan by moving the feed instead of the heavy dish, for example a nodding feed used for height finding while the dish rotates in azimuth. Many simple search radars just rotate the whole antenna. Beamwidth is roughly 70λ/D degrees, where λ is wavelength and D is dish diameter. A search radar often uses a cosecant-squared pattern: gain falls as csc²θ above the horizon. Here θ is elevation angle above the horizon. This gives a more even echo from a target at constant height as its range changes.

A lens antenna bends rays to a focus and can give a shaped beam. A slotted waveguide array is a flat high-gain antenna made of slots cut in a waveguide. A phased array uses many elements and phase shifters. The beam is steered by changing phase, with no moving parts. A passive array shares one transmitter, while an active array has a transmit/receive module at every element. Unit 3 gives the pattern details and Unit 4 gives ferrite and diode phase shifters. A radome covers the antenna and must pass the radar band with low loss.

Transmitters supply short high-power pulses. The magnetron is a crossed-field oscillator that gives high pulse power at low cost; many marine and weather radars use it. A klystron or travelling wave tube (TWT) is an amplifier, so it can follow a stable low-power source and keep phase coherence for MTI. Solid-state transmitters use many gallium nitride (GaN) modules and combine their outputs. They are reliable and need lower voltage, but a single module has modest peak power.

Peak power P<sub>peak</sub> and average power P<sub>avg</sub> are linked by duty cycle: P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>peak</sub> × duty, where duty = τ/T = τ f<sub>prf</sub>. Here τ is pulse width, T is pulse repetition interval and f<sub>prf</sub> is pulse repetition frequency. Cooling must remove the average heat, not the peak. The modulator forms the pulse. A line-type modulator charges a pulse forming network (PFN) and discharges it through a switch into the tube; a hard-tube modulator uses an active tube to shape the pulse. Rise time and flat top matter because they set the pulse spectrum; the smallest usable range is set mainly by the pulse width and the duplexer recovery time. Unit 4 covers tube operation.

The receiver is superheterodyne. A low-noise RF stage sets the noise figure. A mixer converts RF to IF using the STALO, a stable local oscillator. An image-reject filter before the mixer removes the image. IF gain and a detector produce video. A log amplifier compresses a wide dynamic range so weak echoes and strong clutter fit one display. Dynamic range is the ratio of largest to smallest signal handled without distortion. I and Q outputs keep amplitude and phase for Doppler and MTI. CFAR (constant false alarm rate) is a threshold that adapts to the local clutter level. An A-scope plots echo amplitude against range. A B-scope plots range against azimuth. A PPI is a plan view with a rotating sweep. Modern radars use raster displays and scan conversion, with synthetic video from the processor.

The duplexer connects one antenna to the transmitter and the receiver. During transmit, the transmit-receive (TR) tube fires and shorts the receiver; the anti-transmit-receive (ATR) tube detunes the transmitter branch during receive. Gas tubes recover in microseconds. A circulator duplexer uses a ferrite circulator. The isolation needed is I<sub>dB</sub> = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>tx</sub> / P<sub>safe</sub>), where I<sub>dB</sub> is isolation in decibels, P<sub>tx</sub> is transmitter peak power in watts and P<sub>safe</sub> is the maximum power the receiver can absorb in watts. During the pulse, spike leakage can exceed the steady isolation, so a receiver protector clips it. Recovery must be shorter than the round-trip time to the nearest target. In propagation, standard refraction is modelled by a 4/3 earth radius. Ducting traps energy and gives anomalous long-range echoes. Rain attenuates millimetre waves. Near the ground, multipath causes lobing.

spec.aria: Hardware chain: the modulator pulses the transmitter, the duplexer passes the high power to the antenna and then lets the weak echo into the receiver, which mixes it down using the stable local oscillator and sends video to the processor and display.

examples.question: A radar transmitter delivers 100 kW peak power. The receiver front end can safely absorb 10 mW. Find the duplexer isolation needed in decibels. A practical TR tube plus circulator gives 60 to 70 dB. Explain why a receiver protector is still used.
steps: Write the powers in watts: P<sub>tx</sub> = 100 kW = 100 × 10³ W; P<sub>safe</sub> = 10 mW = 10 × 10⁻³ W.
Required power ratio is P<sub>tx</sub> / P<sub>safe</sub> = (100 × 10³) / (10 × 10⁻³) = 1 × 10⁷.
Isolation in decibels is I<sub>dB</sub> = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(1 × 10⁷) = 10 × 7 = 70 dB.
A practical duplexer gives about 60 to 70 dB. The remaining leakage appears as a short spike at the start of the pulse, so a receiver protector clips it.
examples.answer: The duplexer must provide 70 dB of isolation; practical hardware is close to this, so spike leakage still needs a receiver protector.
examples.check:
import math
P_peak = 100e3
P_safe = 10e-3
ratio = P_peak / P_safe
isolation_dB = 10 * math.log10(ratio)
print(ratio)
print(isolation_dB)

traps: Duplexer isolation is not one fixed number for all time. Leakage during the pulse and the recovery period is far larger than in the listening period, so spike leakage and recovery time decide receiver damage and minimum range.
Peak power and average power are not the same. Average power is peak power times duty cycle, and cooling depends on average power.
A magnetron is an oscillator, not an amplifier; a klystron and a TWT are amplifiers that can keep phase coherence.

A cosecant-squared pattern is not a pencil beam. It gives up gain at high elevation angles (near overhead, short range) so that echoes from targets at constant altitude are more uniform as range changes.
A radome is not a simple waterproof cover; a wet or lossy radome can reduce gain and raise sidelobes.

quiz.q: State the job of a duplexer in a radar.
quiz.a: It connects one antenna to the transmitter and the receiver, passing the high-power pulse to the antenna and protecting the receiver from that pulse.

quiz.q: Why does a search radar use a cosecant-squared pattern?
quiz.a: The gain is shaped as csc²θ, so it is reduced at high elevation angles (short slant ranges) and kept high near the horizon. A target at constant height then gives a more even echo as its range changes.

quiz.q: A radar has 50 kW peak power and the receiver safe limit is 5 mW. Find the required isolation in dB.
Why can a high steady isolation still allow receiver damage?
quiz.a: During the pulse, spike leakage is larger than the steady isolation. The receiver protector must clip this short spike.

quiz.q: Why is a STALO used in a radar receiver?
quiz.a: It is a stable local oscillator that mixes the RF echo down to IF, so gain and filtering can be done at a fixed lower frequency.

quiz.q: A TR tube takes 1 μs to recover. What minimum range does this set? Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
quiz.a: Range = c t / 2 = (3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻⁶) / 2 = 150 m. Closer echoes are hidden by the recovery.

quiz.q: What does a PPI display show?
quiz.a: A plan view of targets, with range as radius and azimuth as angle around the screen.

quiz.q: A transmitter has 80 kW peak power and duty cycle 0.001. Find average power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern radar front ends move toward active electronically scanned arrays, with a GaN transmit/receive module behind every element. Digital beamforming and radar-on-chip put more processing close to the antenna. Weather and defence radars use polarimetric and multi-frequency designs to separate targets from clutter. Search for active phased array radar, GaN radar modules and digital beamforming to go further.
